answerKey.primaryProblem: Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (uncontrolled T2DM, dyslipidemia) related to excessive intake of refined carbohydrates/sugar-sweetened beverages and inadequate fiber intake, as evidenced by HbA1c 8.9%, LDL 145 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL, and self-reported diet low in fruits/vegetables/fiber and high in fast food and sugary drinks.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis 1: Excessive carbohydrate/sugar intake (NI-5.8.2) related to habitual sugary beverage and processed food consumption
Nutrition diagnosis 2: Inadequate fiber intake (NI-5.8.5) related to avoidance of fruits/vegetables, contributing to constipation
Nutrition diagnosis 3: Overweight/obesity (NI-1.5/NC-3.3) related to excess energy intake relative to needs and sedentary screen time
Medication-food interaction knowledge deficit affecting metformin adherence (NB-1.1/NB-2.6)
keyFindings: BMI 32.1 kg/m2 (Class I obesity), waist circumference 38 in
Lipid panel: TC 235, LDL 145, HDL 38, TG 180 (all abnormal)
Diet recall: no fruits/vegetables, high refined carbs/sugar, sugary soda intake 2-3/day, skipped breakfast, large late dinner
Constipation reported on direct questioning, likely multifactorial (low fiber, low fluid, possibly medication-related)
Inconsistent metformin adherence due to GI side effects and school schedule; good glipizide adherence
Ambivalent readiness to change; strong motivation tied to soccer performance and appearance, not disease avoidance per se
Barriers: limited cooking skills, cost perceptions, peer/social eating pressure, busy schedule
plan: Nutrition diagnosis/PES statement(s) addressing excessive sugar/refined carb intake and inadequate fiber intake linked to labs and GI symptoms
Collaborative, non-judgmental goal-setting using motivational interviewing — elicit his own reasons tied to soccer performance/energy

Practical, low-barrier substitutions: swap 1 sugary soda/day for water or a diet/zero-sugar option as a first step; add one fruit or vegetable per day with strategies to improve palatability (smoothies, dips, texture modification)
Address constipation with gradual fiber increase (soluble fiber sources less likely to cause bloating) plus increased water intake, paired with reassurance and normalization to reduce embarrassment

Coordinate with prescriber regarding metformin GI side effects — consider extended-release formulation or dose timing adjustment; counsel to take with full meal to reduce nausea rather than skipping doses

Provide budget-friendly, quick-prep meal/snack ideas suitable for a teen with limited cooking skills and time (e.g., batch-prepared items, affordable produce options, pairing protein+fiber for satiety and glycemic control)
Address breakfast skipping and irregular meal timing to support more stable glucose control and reduce large late-night dinners
Discuss sports nutrition specifically — appropriate pre/post-practice fueling without relying on sugary sports drinks/soda
Identify and leverage support system: parents for shopping/meal prep, consider school nutrition services, consider referral to school nurse/counselor given reported absences/declining attention
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess adherence, labs trend (repeat HbA1c in 3 months), and readiness to change; use SMART, patient-generated goals
Screen for and address psychosocial stress and weight-related self-consciousness with empathetic, weight-neutral language focused on performance/health rather than appearance
redFlags: HbA1c 8.9% with symptoms of polyuria/polydipsia and blurred vision suggests ongoing hyperglycemia and risk for progression to insulin requirement/complications if unaddressed
LDL 145 / HDL 38 / TG 180 in an 18-year-old indicate significant cardiovascular risk requiring timely lifestyle intervention
Reported medication non-adherence (metformin) can worsen glycemic control and should be communicated to the prescribing provider
Reported frequent school absences and declining energy/attention (if obtained) warrant interprofessional communication with school nurse and PCP

Chronic constipation with abdominal discomfort should be monitored; rule out red flags (no blood in stool, no severe pain, no weight loss beyond expected) and escalate if it worsens or doesn't improve with dietary measures
educationPoints: Explain in lay terms how refined carbs and sugary drinks drive blood sugar spikes and relate this directly to his soccer performance (crashes/energy dips) to motivate change
Teach practical fiber sources and gradual introduction (to avoid bloating) along with adequate fluid intake to relieve constipation
Clarify that healthy eating does not have to be expensive or require advanced cooking skills; offer concrete low-cost, low-prep examples
Discuss how consistent metformin timing with food can reduce GI side effects, and the importance of not skipping doses without talking to the care team first
Reframe nutrition goals around performance, energy, and control rather than appearance or 'dieting' to reduce defensiveness and support autonomy
Normalize discussing bowel habits as a routine, non-judgmental part of care to reduce his embarrassment

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process to complete a nutrition assessment and formulate an appropriate PES statement reflecting excessive sugar/refined carbohydrate intake and inadequate fiber intake in the context of uncontrolled T2DM and dyslipidemia.

Develop practical, evidence-based nutrition interventions addressing fiber intake, sugar-sweetened beverage reduction, and meal pattern regularity that are feasible given cost, cooking skill, and social barriers.
Integrate medication management considerations into nutrition counseling, including strategies to reduce GI side effects of metformin and support more consistent adherence.

Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore ambivalence, elicit the patient's own motivations (sports performance, energy), and respond empathetically to sensitive topics (weight, bowel habits) without triggering defensiveness.
Identify opportunities for interprofessional collaboration and community/school resources to support this adolescent's nutrition and medical care.

patient.name: Wyatt Nelson
patient.appearance: Appears his stated age, sitting in what looks like his bedroom with soccer posters visible on the wall behind him; wearing a school athletics hoodie; posture slightly hunched, avoids direct eye contact with the camera, gives short answers and glances away when sensitive topics come up.

persona.personality: Shy, sensitive, somewhat guarded; cares about fitting in with teammates and not appearing 'weak' or different
persona.communicationStyle: Concise and short-answered; avoids eye contact especially on sensitive topics; deflects with humor or vague answers when uncomfortable; opens up more with empathetic, non-judgmental, performance-framed questions
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious and self-conscious; a bit defensive about diet and weight; relieved when questions are framed around sports/energy rather than appearance or 'dieting'
persona.background: Wyatt is a senior at a suburban public high school, lives at home with both parents, and plays on the varsity soccer team. He spends a lot of free time gaming online with friends and doing homework. His parents work full-time and are supportive but busy, often relying on takeout or quick meals on weeknights. He was diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes at 15 after a routine physical, and has been followed by his pediatrician and more recently an endocrinologist.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting an initial telehealth nutrition assessment for Wyatt Nelson, an 18-year-old male referred by his endocrinologist for medical nutrition therapy related to uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Review the available chart information before the visit. Conduct a nutrition-focused history (diet, meal pattern, hydration, activity, medication adherence, GI symptoms), identify barriers to change, and use motivational interviewing to engage this ambivalent, self-conscious adolescent. Document your findings using the ADIME format.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia referred for nutrition counseling
scenario.openingLine: Hey... yeah, my doctor said I had to talk to you guys because my blood sugar's not doing great.
tasks: Complete a nutrition-focused assessment including diet history, meal pattern, hydration, physical activity, and anthropometric/lab review
Explore medication adherence barriers (especially metformin GI side effects) and their nutrition implications
Use motivational interviewing to explore the patient's ambivalence and elicit his own motivations (sports performance, energy) for change
Sensitively assess and address constipation/fiber intake without increasing his embarrassment
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) and propose 2-3 realistic, patient-centered interventions, documented in ADIME format

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in his bedroom, calling from a laptop or phone propped on a desk
profile.summary: An 18-year-old male with uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes (HbA1c 8.9%), Class I obesity, dyslipidemia, and constipation presents for an initial telehealth nutrition counseling visit. The case teaches learners to conduct a nutrition-focused assessment, formulate a PES statement, and apply motivational interviewing with a shy, ambivalent adolescent who is sensitive about his weight and bowel habits but motivated by sports performance.
profile.title: Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes and Dyslipidemia in an Ambivalent 18-Year-Old Soccer Player
